opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was a really formative moment for me and for the team. When we first got access to the model, we were genuinely surprised by how much more capable it was than anything we'd worked with before. It was a real step change. The fluency, the reasoning, its ability to take on so many different tasks: that was exciting, but it also meant the risk landscape looked very different.

One of the first things that struck me was that the risks weren't just a longer version of the list we already had. We'd spent years thinking about fairness, about content harms, about things like toxic language in earlier models. Those were all still there. But because the model was so capable and so general, the space of what could go wrong got much bigger. You had to think about people using it to generate convincing misinformation at scale, or about what it means when a system sounds very confident and authoritative but is actually wrong. We came to call that ungrounded content, or hallucination. And then there were new kinds of attacks, like jailbreaks and prompt injection, where people actively try to get the model to step outside its intended behavior.

The other big lesson was that red teaming the raw model by itself wasn't enough. What really matters is the model in the context of the application. A risk can look very different in a search experience compared to a coding assistant or a customer service bot. So we quickly realized that we needed a layered approach. You have mitigations at the model level, but also safety systems around it: content filters, metaprompts or system messages that steer behavior, and grounding in reliable data. Then there's the user experience design, things like being transparent that you're talking to an AI and making it easy to check sources.

It also showed me that this couldn't be a one-time exercise. We'd red team, find issues, put mitigations in place, and then find new issues as we got creative, or as the model changed. So it really pushed us toward building measurement at scale. We couldn't rely only on humans manually probing the system. We needed automated ways to evaluate risks continuously, and actually we ended up using the models themselves to help with that.

So in a lot of ways, that early experience shaped the whole playbook we've used since: map the risks, measure them systematically, mitigate in layers, and keep operating and monitoring once it's out in the world. It made it very concrete for us that responsible AI has to be engineered into the product from the beginning, not added at the end.

r001.rationale: The response names several risk areas and says the team needed to map risks systematically, but it does not describe organizing red-teaming findings across those areas into a risk taxonomy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it was actually a pretty surreal experience. We got early access to GPT-4 at Microsoft, and the first thing we did was sit down with it, and I remember just being struck by how different it was. The capabilities had jumped so much from the previous generation, and I had this moment of, "Okay, everything we thought we knew about where the risks are, we need to go back and re-examine."

And I think what the red teaming really taught me is that the risks don't scale linearly with capability. Some of the issues we'd worked hard on with earlier models, like obvious toxic outputs, were actually easier to manage because the model was so much better at following instructions. But that same capability opened up entirely new categories of problems. The model could be persuasive, it could be convincingly wrong, it could reason its way around guardrails in ways you didn't anticipate. So the surface area changed rather than just getting bigger or smaller.

The other thing that really hit home was that you can't do this from your desk alone. We brought in people with very different backgrounds, people who think about security, people who think about social harms, domain experts in things like medicine or chemistry. Every one of them found something the rest of us missed, because they were probing from a completely different mental model of how someone might misuse the system. And that's shaped how we approach it at Microsoft now. Red teaming isn't a checkbox you do once before launch. It's an ongoing practice, it's multidisciplinary, and frankly it's humbling, because every time you think you've understood the model, it surprises you.

So I came away thinking about risk less as a list of known failure modes and more as a discipline of continuous discovery. You have to assume there are things you haven't found yet, and you build your mitigation layers and your monitoring with that assumption baked in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses new risk categories and findings from multidisciplinary red teaming, but does not say the findings were organized into a risk taxonomy.

astra-6.text:
What really stood out to me was that you couldn’t separate the risks from the capabilities. The same ability to follow a complicated request and generate a convincing response could be incredibly useful, but it could also make a harmful response more consequential.

That changed how I thought about testing. It wasn’t enough to ask, “Can we get the model to say something bad?” We needed to ask, “What could someone accomplish with this, in what context, and what safeguards would actually help?” And we needed people with different perspectives probing those questions, because no single team is going to anticipate every way a system might be used.

The takeaway for me was that red teaming has to be an ongoing process. It helps you discover risks and improve mitigations, but it isn’t a certificate that the system is safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses risks, contexts, safeguards, and varied perspectives, but does not describe organizing red-teaming findings across multiple areas into a risk taxonomy.

sol-6.1.text:
What stood out to me was that you couldn’t understand the risks just by looking at how the model behaved in a normal conversation. You had to actively probe it: change the framing, challenge its boundaries, and think about how someone might misuse its capabilities.

That also meant looking beyond the model’s response to the context in which it would be used. Who’s interacting with it? What information or tools can it access? What happens if it gets something wrong? Red teaming helped me think about risk as a property of the whole system, and about safety as an ongoing process rather than a test you pass once.

r001.rationale: The response describes probing model behavior and considering system-level risks, but it does not say findings from multiple red-teaming areas were organized into a risk taxonomy.
